name: Airframe
blurb: Structures and aerodynamics: simulation, analysis, CAD and machining. The airframe has to survive peak loading and come back straight.
detail: Airframe designs and analyzes every structural part of the rocket: the body tube, fin can, nosecone, and the load paths between them. Work starts in CAD and OpenRocket, where the subteam models flight performance and aerodynamic behaviour before anything gets cut or laid up. Airframe works closely with Avionics, Payload, and Composites through the build, since its decisions set the envelope everyone else designs into: what fits inside the tube, how sections mate, and what the structure can survive under peak loading and landing.
first: Help translate an OpenRocket or Onshape model into a part you can machine or lay up, and shadow fin sanding, body-tube rolling, or a structural load test. First projects are hands-on shop work tied to whatever the current airframe needs.
skills: OpenRocket, Onshape, and basic structural intuition. Ansys helps if you want to run FEA. CAD and machining experience are useful but not required; we teach the rest.
photoAlt: A team member at the lathe, one hand on the Colchester carriage handwheel and safety glasses on, with the tool post and swarf on the bed in front of him.
photoCaption: Machining a fitting on the lathe. Most structural hardware starts here before it goes in the tube.

name: Avionics
blurb: Flight computers and telemetry: embedded firmware and PCB design in KiCad. This subteam decides when every event on the flight fires.
detail: Avionics builds the flight computer stack: the sensors that tell the rocket where it is, the logic that decides when to fire each event, and the telemetry that gets the data back to the ground. Competition rules require a commercial altimeter and GPS as the primary flight computer, currently a Blue Raven paired with a Featherweight GPS. Alongside that, the subteam designs its own SRAD boards in KiCad, such as Void Lake, which fly as backup. There is also mechanical work if you want it: mounts, harnesses, and how boards and wiring sit in the airframe. If you have written code before, this is the fastest place on the team to see your work fly. If you have not, this is where a lot of us learned.
first: Shadow a flight-computer build, start a board in KiCad, wire and test one sensor, and help run a ground test. No prior hardware experience assumed.
skills: C or Python, KiCad, a soldering iron you are not afraid of, and any exposure to control theory. CAD helps if you want to work on how boards and wiring attach to the internal structure. We teach the rest.
photoAlt: Hands wiring an open avionics bay on the workbench: coloured harnesses, a circuit board with red indicator LEDs, and tools laid out beside it.
photoCaption: Wiring the bay on the bench. The harnesses go in before the tube closes.

name: Propulsion
blurb: Motor integration, thrust curves, and Icarus: our in-house hybrid engine in development alongside the commercial motors we fly today.
detail: Propulsion handles commercial motor selection and integration for the competition airframe each year: reload cases, thrust curves, and the hardware that holds the motor in the tube. Alongside that, the subteam develops Icarus, the team's in-house hybrid engine (N₂O and paraffin wax), with static fires and Tech-Dev Challenge entries at Launch Canada. Day to day that means test-stand work, fuel casting, injector and chamber design, and the safety procedures that come with working on live propellants.
first: Shadow a motor install in the airframe, help prep a fuel grain or test fixture, and sit in on a cold-flow or static-fire test day. No prior propulsion experience needed; safety training comes first.
skills: MATLAB or Python for thrust and chamber sizing, CAD for mounts and test hardware, and comfort following written procedures in the shop. Chemistry or mechanical background helps for Icarus; COTS integration is mostly mechanical.
photoAlt: CAD render of the Icarus hybrid engine test stand: 80/20 aluminum extrusion frame with a horizontal oxidizer tank and vertical combustion chamber assembly.
photoCaption: Icarus test stand in CAD. Propulsion bolts the fill system, chamber, and instrumentation here before cold-flow and static-fire tests.

name: Recovery
blurb: Dual-deployment parachutes and the sequencing that brings the vehicle back intact.
detail: Recovery runs dual deployment: a drogue chute at apogee to slow the descent, then the main parachute lower down to cut drift and bring the airframe down intact. Black powder charges, triggered by signals from Avionics, fire both stages. Deployment currently rides on commercial hardware, a Featherweight Blue Raven altimeter as primary with an EasyMini as backup, alongside a Featherweight GPS for tracking. The subteam also writes the simulation code that predicts apogee and terminal velocity under different parachute sizes, and checks those predictions against real launch data. Recovery also did the mechanical design for the airbrakes flown on Nimbus and Osiris.
first: Help pack and inspect a parachute, and shadow a ground deployment test using black powder charges. No pyrotechnics experience needed; the process is taught on the team.
skills: Comfort with basic electronics and wiring, and some Python or MATLAB if you want to work on the simulation code. CAD helps for chute bays and shock cord mounts. We teach the rest.
photoAlt: CAD wireframe of the airbrake mechanism: a cylindrical housing with linkage arms and two curved drag plates extended from the sides.
photoCaption: Airbrake assembly for Nimbus and Osiris. Recovery designed the mechanism; Avionics commands deployment.

name: Payload
blurb: The experiment we fly, and most years the reason the rocket exists at all. CAD, electrical and software all sit on it.
detail: Payload designs, builds, and integrates the experiment or technical demonstration the rocket carries each year, most years the reason the rocket flies at all. It sits alongside Airframe, which has to make the payload fit and survive flight, and Avionics, which handles triggering over the CAN bus. Recent payloads: Magpie (2026), an SRAD fracture test module carrying epoxy test articles to measure how a self-healing polymer performs in flight, which took first place in the Payload Challenge at Launch Canada; Sparrow (2025), a 360-degree camera with a recovery beacon that also took first place at Launch Canada; and a 2024 first-person-view camera system recording flight at 2K and 60 frames per second.
first: Help build and test one part of the current payload, whether that's the mechanical housing, the electronics, or the software that runs it. The payload changes every year, so the first project you touch is whatever that season's experiment needs.
skills: Depends on the year's payload: CAD and machining for the housing, embedded C for the electronics, or materials science for an experiment like Magpie's polymer test. No single background is required.
photoAlt: Magpie electronics stack on the bench: three SRAD boards in a nylon frame, powered on with status LEDs lit.
photoCaption: Bench bring-up on the Magpie SRAD stack. The boards talk over CAN before the tube closes.

name: Composites
blurb: Carbon and fibreglass layup, tooling, and the finishing that makes it fly straight.
detail: Composites turns CAD into flight-ready parts: nose cones, body tubes, carbon fins, and the jigs that hold them straight during layup. Most exposed airframe surfaces are fibreglass or carbon fibre rolled and cured in-house rather than bought off the shelf. The subteam works from Airframe's models, advises on what will lay up cleanly, and owns final assembly once the parts are out of the mould.
first: Help roll a body tube, trim a fin in the mould, or prep a layup under a lead's supervision. First projects are hands-on shop work, not theory.
skills: Patience with epoxy and PPE, attention to finish quality, and basic CAD literacy so you can read the parts you're making. Prior composites experience is rare on the team; we teach the process.
photoAlt: Team members around a vacuum chamber in the composites bay: one films the setup on a phone while others monitor the laptop and gauge.
photoCaption: Vacuum bagging a layup. Pressure pulls the bag tight so every ply bonds without voids.

name: Operations
blurb: Graphic design, merch, and social media. What people see when they have never set foot in the shop.
detail: Operations is the subteam behind McMaster Rocketry's public face. Members design merch and competition graphics, shoot build nights and pad footage, and run the team's Instagram, LinkedIn, and Discord. Outreach booths at Clubfest and Facultyfest, and the materials that go to sponsors, all build on the same look. If you want your work worn on campus or posted the morning after a launch, start here.
first: Design a sticker or tee graphic, shoot and edit footage from a build night, or help plan and post a week of launch content. Your first project is usually one concrete piece: a design, a reel, or a booth shift.
skills: Illustration, graphic design, photography, or video editing. Writing helps for social copy and sponsor outreach. Figma, Illustrator, or similar. We teach the rest.
photoAlt: Osiris carbon-fibre fins covered in gold team signatures on the competition table.
photoCaption: Signed fins at Launch Canada. Merch and graphics start with moments like this.
